# FAA AI Safety Roadmap — Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Safety Assurance, Version I

> **External, not NASA governance.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary. It never establishes
> what NASA requires, and must not be cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Office of Aviation Safety |
| **Kind** | Agency roadmap / guidance (non-binding) |
| **Status** | "Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Safety Assurance, Version I," signed 2024-07-23 by David H. Boulter, Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety. Self-described in its closing section (p.30 of 31, FAA's own footer numbering) as "a point-in-time snapshot of a fast-paced and evolving technology" — a living document, not a final framework. |
| **Where to get it** | Public, faa.gov; public copy, confirmed anonymously off-network on 2026-10-26: `https://www.faa.gov/media/82891` |
| **Binds whom** | No one directly. A roadmap of guiding principles and mostly-TBD planned instruments; the only near-term applicant-facing item is a disclosure requirement ("tell us you're using AI, early"), itself still a draft milestone (p.27 of 31). |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** This is the sibling civil-aviation regulator's
own roadmap-stage AI document, and a natural pattern for NASA to compare against (our reading). It is useful for vocabulary (its seven guiding principles) and for an honest picture of how
little is actually settled even in an agency further along than NASA on this question — most of its
own concrete deliverables are scheduled "TBD" (our reading).

**Key content for AI / machine-learning assurance.**
- Seven "Guiding Principles," verbatim titles (p.7–8 of 31): Work Within the Aviation Ecosystem; Focus
  on Safety Assurance and Safety Enhancements; Avoid Personification; Differentiate Between Learned and
  Learning AI; Take an Incremental Approach; Leverage the Safety Continuum; Leverage Industry Consensus
  Standards.
- Names "Overarching Properties" (intent / correctness / innocuity) as a NASA-originated (Holloway,
  2022) conceptual framework the FAA is co-exploring with NASA (p.20–21 of 31). 🔴 **Verified: the
  roadmap never defines any of the three terms**, and its own cross-reference to "section 5.3" (p.25 of
  31) points to a section number that does not exist anywhere in the document — confirmed independently
  twice (by page read and by whole-document term search).
- Distinguishes "Learned AI Implementation" (static, trained offline, p.10 of 31) from "Learning AI
  Implementation" (dynamic, adapts during operation, p.10 of 31); explicitly deprioritizes safety-
  assurance research for Learning AI, stating it is "likely to remain in the discovery readiness level
  for more than three years" (p.23 of 31).
- Points to the pre-existing Design Assurance Level (DAL) scale (sourced to DO-178C, footnote 5, p.12 of
  31) and the "Safety Continuum" (risk-by-operation-type) as its actual consequence-tiering mechanisms,
  rather than inventing a new one.
- Names SAE G-34 as a new AI-specific industry standard the FAA is "supporting the development of"
  (p.22 of 31).
- Explicit scope exclusions, each stated in the document's own words: ethics (p.3 of 31), broader
  societal aspects (p.8 of 31), airspace efficiency (p.18 of 31).

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** Compares to `../documents/NPR_7150.2D.md` and `../documents/NASA-HDBK-2203.md`
as a sibling agency's roadmap-stage document; as of this reading, neither NASA nor FAA has an adopted,
AI-specific binding standard (our reading).
